title: Lifting Lifted Product Codes
abstract: Lifted product (LP) codes form an important class of quantum error correcting codes with favorable code parameters. We introduce a systematic construction of LP code families based on group extensions and graph lifts. The construction increases the code size while preserving the local structure of the Tanner graph, and relates code parameters, logical operators, and fault-tolerant logical-operation gadgets within the families through chain and cochain maps.   As a first application, we obtain LP codes with better code parameters than previously reported ones. We then demonstrate that code-surgery gadgets can be transferred across the selected finite lifts through chain maps and, in several cases, implemented with lower space overhead. We also develop parallel product surgery for lifted clustered cyclic codes. Finally, we propose lifting as a systematic first step toward defining thermodynamic families for algebraically defined qLDPC codes without an underlying Euclidean lattice. For several base codes and selected lifts, coherent information exhibits finite-size crossings, while our results also indicate that additional conditions are needed to determine a unique family.
summary: This paper presents a systematic algebraic construction method to generate families of Lifted Product quantum error correcting codes by utilizing group extensions and graph lifts. This framework allows researchers to systematically search for better code parameters and define thermodynamic limits for qLDPC codes without relying on Euclidean lattices. It advances the theoretical understanding of scalable, fault-tolerant quantum memory.
main_problem: To develop a systematic method for constructing families of Lifted Product (LP) quantum error correcting codes (qLDPC codes) by generalizing existing constructions.
main_result: The authors introduce a construction based on group extensions that yields LP codes with improved parameters and provides a framework to define thermodynamic families for algebraically defined qLDPC codes.
method: The core method involves using algebraic tools like group extensions and graph lifts applied to the underlying Tanner graphs, relating code properties via chain and cochain maps.
model_or_system: The system is quantum error correcting codes, specifically Lifted Product (LP) codes, which are analyzed using their associated Tanner graphs and defined over free modules of group algebras ($	ext{F}_2[G]$).
key_observables: Code parameters ($J_{12}, 2, 3K$), local incidence structure of the Tanner graph, and coherent information ($\mathcal{I}$).
important_parameters: The structure depends on group extensions $	ext{1} 	o K \xrightarrow{\chi} H \xrightarrow{\pi} G 	o 	ext{1}$ and the choice of section $\sigma$.
main_assumptions: While lifting preserves local structure, additional conditions are necessary to guarantee a unique thermodynamic family; the general construction does not always yield an LP code.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the lift of a Tanner graph while preserving local incidence structure. Figure 2 details the local structures for both the base and lifted codes over different group algebras.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the algebraic framework for lifting and projecting LP codes between different group algebras, proving structural relationships via chain/cochain maps before applying this to derive new code families and analyze physical observables like coherent information.
why_interesting: Although focused on abstract coding theory, the rigorous mathematical structure developed (group extensions, homological algebra) is highly relevant for understanding the stability and generalization of quantum codes used in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

The base (lifted) LP code is a cyclic code defined by the cyclic group Z6 (Z18), respectively. The bound- ary maps are given by HA = � x + x2 and HB = � x + x−1 in both cases. FIG. 3. Normalized space cost of direct code surgery and the lifted code surgery. The horizontal axis shows the number of logical operators measured, and the vertical axis shows the normalized space cost, which is the total num- ber of qubits and checks in the merged code divided by that of the data code. We randomly select five sets of m logi- cal operators for each m = 1, . . . , 12, whose normalized space cost fluctuates across the sets as shown using the error bars. The dashed lines show the space overhead after initialization, whereas solid lines indicate the overhead after the estimated distance has been restored.
